title: Pauquacumsuck / Pahquahkossit (Wading River)
summary: Wading River’s Indigenous name connects the creek with quahog gathering and Native knowledge of the coastal landscape. Paucamp’s 1660 testimony preserves that connection, while later Native-led church history shows community life continuing beyond the colonial deeds.
map_geometry_source: USGS station 01304100, Wading River at Wading River, NY; WGS84 stream coordinates. Geographic orientation only, not a historic settlement or public access point. Checked September 17, 2026.
why_this_matters: Unearthing early pre-fishtail arrowheads, archaeologists identified Pahquahkossit as an Archaic period winter camp occupied as early as 2595 BC along the sheltered banks of present-day Wading River. Documenting such seasonal habitation sites demonstrates how Indigenous extended families successfully utilized and adapted to Long Island's specific ecological zones over thousands of years.
introduction_content: Pauquacumsuck is connected with the creek now known as Wading River in Riverhead, and earlier Pahquahkossit is one of its related historical forms.
history_content:
In testimony recorded in 1660, the elder Paucamp described the Occabauk boundary reaching a wading creek on the North Shore. He explained that the name Pequaockeon referred to the quahogs found there. William Wallace Tooker reproduced this account in 1911 and related the longer Pauquacumsuck forms to clam gathering and an outlet. The testimony places Native environmental knowledge at the center of the name’s history.1

Native leadership after the land records

Wading River also belonged to a network of eighteenth-century Native congregations. Historian John A. Strong describes Peter John Cuffee helping form small parishes at Wading River, Shinnecock, and Islip after beginning his work at Poospatuck. Strong interprets the locally autonomous Congregational organization as important to Native and African American parishioners, who could choose their own ministers. This history adds Native leadership and community-building to a story too often told only through land sales.2

Resources remembered by Shinnecock elders

The Shinnecock Environmental Department’s 2014 catalogue names Wading River bays in its resource accounts. These sections preserve the places named in that 2014 community record. Present-day access, abundance, and harvesting rules may differ.

Bluefish

The catalogue follows bluefish from spring into late fall and describes the bays as feeding and breeding waters. Its attention to season and water conditions records knowledge built through repeated fishing. PDF p. 2.

Flounder

The elders’ catalogue identifies the southern bay bottoms with seasonal flounder fishing. The entry treats the bay floor as a living part of the community’s food landscape. PDF p. 3.

American shad

The catalogue places shad in both food and planting traditions. Fish arriving in spring are part of a seasonal relationship also recalled in the shadbush entry, where flowering signaled the time to prepare for shad fishing. PDF p. 3.

Explore all resources and places in the catalogue.

Shinnecock Environmental Department, Natural Resources Identified by Shinnecock Elders, April 4, 2014, PDF pp. 2–3. Page numbers count the cover as PDF page 1.
translation_content:
Recorded forms include Pequaockeon, Quaconsuck, Pauquaconsut, Pauquaconsuck, Paquaconsit, Pauquacumsok, Pauquacumsuck, Pahquahkossit, and Pahquahokossit. The name is interpreted as the brook or outlet where people wade for clams, or a clam-wading brook.

Why Place Names Matter

“When conditions change, place names can serve as indicators of environmental change.”

— Arctic Climate Impact Assessment, Changing Arctic: Indigenous Perspectives (2005), Box 3.2, 'Place names as indicators of environmental change', PDF page 66

Documenting such seasonal habitation sites demonstrates how Indigenous extended families successfully utilized and adapted to Long Island's specific ecological zones over thousands of years.
vandalism_content: It is believed that Pahquahkossit has been completely destroyed by the new decommissioned Shoreham Nuclear Powerplant.
whereintheworld_content:
The pin follows the modern Wading River waterway, using the U.S. Geological Survey’s mapped stream location at Wading River. It provides orientation to the creek, not directions to a historic settlement, harvesting place, chapel, or public entrance. The USGS coordinates are interpolated from a map and have a stated accuracy of about one arc-second.3

Tooker identifies the creek with modern Wading River, but the historical sources do not survey the exact location of gathering places or the later Native congregation. Follow posted access rules and stay on public roads and paths.

Reading the marsh outline

The shaded area follows a modern mapped marsh beside Wading River. It helps show the wetland landscape associated with the creek, while the dot retains the USGS stream reference. It is not an exact outline of Pauquacumsuck’s historical extent, a settlement, or a tribal boundary. Smaller upstream channels and surrounding uplands are not included.4
